findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. They can answer "what is it" and "why does it matter" before they scroll.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The next step is concrete. It lists the prerequisites, the clone command, the install command and a first command to try, and a link near the top jumps straight there.
findings.source: Heading "Next steps": "git clone https://github.com/doodla/athena.git", "./setup.sh", "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The site is Athena's home page, but almost all of the content is a detailed study of another project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to understand that this page is a sample of Athena's output, not documentation for Athena. Only the third lede paragraph makes that clear.
findings.source: Title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and "This page is that study of firstmate."

findings.text: This link is aimed at the project owner, but it sits in the header that newcomers read first. Someone new would not know whose decisions are meant or whether the link applies to them.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The body is dense and technical: states, counters, transitions and guards. That suits someone checking firstmate's internals, but it is far more than a newcomer needs to judge Athena. They will probably skim it or stop reading.
findings.source: Heading "Transitions": twelve cards t1–t12 with Trigger/Guard/Failure fields, e.g. "t7 close-pending → close-pending"

findings.text: Each state appears only as a name, a tag and claim ids, so to learn what a state means the reader has to look it up in the glossary further down.
findings.source: Heading "States of a piece of work": "queued initial", "ready waiting"

findings.text: The early definitions use terms before defining them: "green" is defined in terms of "red", which only appears in the next entry. Also, "in scope" is defined but openly has no test.
findings.source: "Words used first": "green — A PR that is not red" listed before "red"

findings.text: The page says plainly that nothing was run and every claim comes from reading the source. Together with the per-claim source links, this supports the page's own pitch that Athena's work is traceable.
findings.source: Heading "Limits of this study": "This study read the pinned tree only... no failure or retry edge was observed"

findings.text: This mentions a studies/ folder without saying which repository it is in, so a newcomer cannot follow it.
findings.source: Heading "About this page": "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data"
